title: Privileged Access Management
summary: Privileged access management (PAM) is the discipline and tooling set that controls, brokers, records and audits the use of accounts with elevated rights, including domain administrators, root, database superusers, cloud root and organisation owner roles, and the service accounts that hold equivalent power. The core problem PAM addresses is that privileged credentials are shared, rarely rotated, widely copied into scripts and configuration files, and almost never attributable to an individual, so a single disclosure can be replayed indefinitely with the full authority of the account. A mature programme removes standing privilege wherever possible by vaulting credentials and checking them out for a bounded window, injecting them into sessions so the human never sees the secret, brokering interactive sessions through a jump host that records keystrokes and commands, and replacing human-held credentials with short-lived certificates or tokens. Just-in-time elevation, approval workflows and break-glass procedures with mandatory post-use review are the mechanisms that make this workable when a human genuinely needs emergency access. Beyond vaulting, PAM covers the secrets that machines use: application credentials, API keys and certificates stored in a managed vault with automatic rotation rather than committed to repositories or baked into images. The detection value is substantial, because privileged session recordings, checkout logs and vault audit trails give defenders a well-defined baseline against which unusual hours, unusual source hosts, direct use of an unvaulted credential, or elevation outside the approved workflow stand out sharply.
objectives: You will be able to inventory privileged identities across on-premises, cloud and database estates and classify them by blast radius.
You will be able to design credential checkout, session brokering and rotation workflows that eliminate standing privilege.
You will be able to explain how session recording, keystroke logging and command-level auditing support investigation and attribution.
You will be able to define break-glass access procedures with approval, time bounds and mandatory post-incident review.
You will be able to detect use of unvaulted credentials, out-of-window elevation and anomalous privileged session sources.
You will be able to extend PAM controls to service accounts, API keys and certificates with automated rotation.

beginner.definition: Privileged access management, or PAM, is the set of tools and habits that control powerful accounts. These accounts can change systems, read any data, and create new administrators. PAM stores their passwords safely, hands them out briefly, and records what happens.
beginner.whyItMatters: Powerful passwords are often shared, copied into scripts, and never changed. Nobody can say who used them. One leak then gives an attacker lasting control of everything. PAM fixes this by keeping secrets in a vault and giving each person a named, time-limited session. The audit trail also tells you what really happened.
howItWorks: You list every powerful account, including service accounts that machines use.
Passwords move into a vault, which is a protected store with strict access.
You check out a password for a short window, or the tool types it for you.
Your session runs through a jump host, which records the commands you use.
The password is rotated when you return it, so the old value stops working.
beginner.example: Think of the keys to a building. In a careless office, ten people copy the master key and nobody knows who has one. In a careful office, the key hangs in a locked cabinet. You sign it out, use it, and return it the same day. A camera records the corridor. If something goes wrong, the sign-out book answers the question.
takeaways: Powerful credentials should live in a vault, not in scripts or notes.
Give named, short sessions so every action has an owner.
Record privileged sessions, because recordings settle arguments during investigations.
